title: Conditional Probability and Counting
description: Comprehensive shared preparation notes and worked practice for Conditional Probability and Counting. Review the target examination syllabus and level before reuse.

sections.label: Concepts and worked examples
sections.html:
Conditional probability

The probability of A given B is (\(P(A|B)=P(A \cap B)/P(B)\)), provided (\(P(B)>0\)). Conditioning restricts the sample space to outcomes where B occurred.

Multiplication and independence

The multiplication rule is (\(P(A \cap B)=P(A|B)P(B)\)). Events are independent when (\(P(A|B)=P(A)\)); equivalently, (\(P(A \cap B)=P(A)P(B)\)). Drawing without replacement generally makes successive outcomes dependent.

Bayes theorem

For mutually exclusive and exhaustive causes (B_i), (\(P(B_j|A)=P(A|B_j)P(B_j)/\sum_i P(A|B_i)P(B_i)\)). Separate prior probability from the likelihood of the observed evidence.

Worked example: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue balls. Without replacement, after drawing a red ball, 2 red remain among 4 balls. Thus the probability the next ball is red, given the first was red, is (\(2/4=1/2\)).

sections.label: Methods and exam checks
sections.html:
• Rewrite the condition in words: the denominator is the event already known to have occurred.
  • Use a tree diagram for sequential events and label branch probabilities at each stage.
  • For without replacement, update counts after each draw.
  • For reverse-conditioning questions, use Bayes theorem and include all possible causes in the denominator.
  • Check probabilities remain between 0 and 1 and branch totals equal 1.

sections.label: Key facts and formulas
sections.html:
• (\(P(A|B)=P(A \cap B)/P(B)\)).
  • Independent events satisfy (\(P(A \cap B)=P(A)P(B)\)).
  • Mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities are not independent.
  • Complement: (\(P(A^c)=1-P(A)\)).

sections.label: Worked practice
sections.html:
1. Core:

    A fair die is rolled. Given that the result is even, what is the probability it is greater than 3?

    1. (\(1/3\))
    2. (\(1/2\))
    3. (\(2/3\))
    4. (\(1\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(2/3\))

    The conditioned outcomes are (\({2,4,6}\)); those greater than 3 are (\({4,6}\)). Probability (\(=2/3\)).

  2. Core:

    A bag has 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two are drawn without replacement. Given the first is red, what is the chance the second is red?

    1. (\(1/5\))
    2. (\(1/2\))
    3. (\(3/5\))
    4. (\(2/3\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(1/2\))

    After one red is removed, 2 red counters remain among 4 counters, so the probability is (\(2/4=1/2\)).

  3. Foundation:

    A card is known to be a face card in a standard deck. What is the probability it is a king?

    1. (\(1/13\))
    2. (\(1/4\))
    3. (\(1/3\))
    4. (\(4/13\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(1/3\))

    There are 12 face cards (J, Q, K) and 4 are kings. The conditional probability is (\(4/12=1/3\)).

  4. Standard:

    A bag has 4 green and 3 yellow balls. Two are drawn without replacement. Given the first is green, what is the probability the second is green?

    1. (\(1/2\))
    2. (\(3/7\))
    3. (\(2/3\))
    4. (\(4/7\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(1/2\))

    After a green is removed, 3 green remain among 6 balls. Probability is (\(3/6=1/2\)).

  5. Challenge:

    A disease affects 1% of a population. A test is positive for 90% of affected people and 5% of unaffected people. Given a positive result, what is the probability of disease?

    1. (\(2/13\))
    2. (\(9/59\))
    3. (\(1/2\))
    4. (\(9/10\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(2/13\))

    Bayes numerator is (\(0.01 \times 0.90=0.009\)). Positive probability is (\(0.009+0.99 \times 0.05=0.0585\)). Thus the probability is (\(0.009/0.0585=2/13\)).
